nodes.label: Detachment as precondition
nodes.summary: True understanding of the Prophets requires inner detachment. The argument which follows cannot be received by a heart still measuring them by ordinary human standards.

nodes.label: The true standard of recognition
nodes.summary: God's Messengers cannot be recognized by the standards of ordinary people. Judging them by human words and deeds is the root of rejection in every age.

nodes.label: The historical pattern of rejection
nodes.summary: In every age the Promised One is awaited — and denied by the very people who awaited Him. Noah and Húd are the first cases; the Abrahamic line and Muḥammad continue the pattern.

nodes.label: The Abrahamic line as further witness
nodes.summary: Placeholder. Ṣáliḥ, Ibrāhīm, Mūsā, and ʿĪsā — each faces the same denial from the generation meant to recognize Him. The pattern is structural, not incidental.

nodes.label: Muḥammad and the People of the Book
nodes.summary: Placeholder. The Jews and Christians who had awaited a Promised One and yet rejected Muḥammad — a case especially pointed to the reader, since the Qur'an itself records it.

nodes.label: Objection: the signs of the Day have not appeared
nodes.summary: Placeholder. The Qur'an foretells sun darkening, clouds, stars falling, the Hour. None of this has happened literally, so the Manifestation cannot have come.

nodes.label: Response: the signs are to be read symbolically
nodes.summary: Placeholder. Bahá'u'lláh's central interpretive move: the cosmological imagery of the Qur'an speaks of a spiritual reality, not a physical one.

nodes.label: The Qur'an's own distinction of clear and allegorical verses
nodes.summary: Placeholder. The hermeneutic is not imposed on the Qur'an from outside — it is the Qur'an's own distinction in 3:7 between muḥkam (clear) and mutashābih (allegorical) verses.

nodes.label: What "sun", "cloud", "star" mean
nodes.summary: Placeholder. The sun as the Manifestation, the clouds as that which veils Him, the stars as the divines of the former dispensation. Each image is given a spiritual referent grounded in scripture.

nodes.label: The meaning of "return"
nodes.summary: Placeholder. John the Baptist as the "return" of Elijah is the scriptural key. "Return" names a return of station and quality, not of individual person.

nodes.label: Objection: Muḥammad is the Seal of the Prophets
nodes.summary: Placeholder. The Qur'an names Muḥammad Khātam al-Nabiyyīn. Therefore no Manifestation can come after Him. This is the central Islamic objection the book addresses.

nodes.label: Response: the station of the Manifestations is one
nodes.summary: Placeholder. The Prophets share a single station; their outward differences are conditioned by time and audience. "Seal" is read as denoting a station of culmination within a cycle, not an absolute termination of revelation.

nodes.label: Objection: the signs of the Qá'im were not fulfilled
nodes.summary: Placeholder. The Qá'im was expected in a specific line, with specific outward signs — the sword, the banner, global dominion. None of this appears literally.

nodes.label: Response: the signs of the Qá'im are also to be re-read
nodes.summary: Placeholder. The same hermeneutic of clear and allegorical, already established from the Qur'an, applies to the ḥadīth concerning the Qá'im.

nodes.label: The Qur'an as the standard of judgment
nodes.summary: Placeholder. The book closes by returning the reader to the Qur'an itself as the criterion. The reader is not asked to accept Bahá'u'lláh's conclusions on authority — they are asked to weigh them by the Qur'an.
